Use an ability to hit both the wave and an opponent when the angle allows it. Wave pressure makes the enemy choose between collecting souls and answering your damage. If you cannot trade safely, secure the wave and improve your position before trying again.

Track the spell or movement tool that would punish your approach. Use a small commitment to test the response rather than spending every cooldown at once. Some spirit carries are strong lane aggressors, but that is not permission to force every matchup or every low-health chase.
For the shared fundamentals, read the [Deadlock laning guide](/guides/laning-counterplay).

Turn lane pressure into a useful movement window. If you push the enemy back, you may be able to rotate with a teammate or threaten accessible enemy resources. Check visibility and travel time before leaving; a possible invade is not worth surrendering an undefended objective.

Collect farm between opportunities so your damage keeps pace. You should not roam empty-handed while your spells are unavailable or every target is protected. A cleared wave gives both resources and information about where pressure can move next.

Coordinate an aggressive route with someone who can catch a target or cover your exit. If your combo needs an enemy to stay still, a pick teammate makes that window more reliable. If your hero controls ground through summons or zones, use that pressure to deny an approach rather than forcing a dive.

Choose an angle that lets your damage reach a useful target. Wait for control, defensive spells or movement to be spent when they would otherwise deny the combo. Keep sight of your teammates so your opening can become a finish instead of an isolated trade.

Treat damage and escape abilities as separate decisions even when the same spell does both. On a mobile hero, spending all movement to reach the backline can remove the only way out. On an area-control hero, abandoning prepared ground may throw away your strongest fighting position.

Between damage windows, change your angle, use cover and watch the next target rather than standing exposed while waiting for cooldowns. Re-enter when a spell is available and the target can be reached.
How to choose items for your role

Choose investment that supports the damage pattern you actually use: burst, repeated hits or sustained area pressure. Avoid copying a burst build onto a role that needs to stay in the fight for longer.

[Healbane](/counter-items/healbane) can fit repeated spirit application when healing is the problem. A movement or control answer may be more useful when the enemy survives by escaping. Compare [mobility counters](/guides/mobility) and [counter-buy priorities](/guides/counter-itemization) before adding several situational items.
Use the [Counter Item Helper](/counter-item-helper) to compare answers to the enemy heroes, then choose the purchase that fits your job.
Spending the full combo before the enemy uses their defensive tool.
Invading without visibility, wave pressure or nearby help.
Using every escape for damage and becoming the easiest target to catch.
Treating every spirit hero as a close-range burst assassin.

On Pocket, consider whether you need Briefcase or the cloak route to survive the next response before using it for damage. The strongest damage sequence is the one that leaves you able to keep contributing afterward.
[Back to the full hero roles chart →](/roles)
Is spirit carry the same as spirit nuker?

They overlap. Spirit nuker usually highlights burst damage, while spirit carry can also include repeated spell pressure or area damage. Follow the damage pattern and responsibilities of your actual build.
Should spirit carries farm or roam?
Do both with purpose. Collect resources between useful cooldown windows and rotate when lane pressure, visibility and nearby help give you a realistic opportunity.
Can a spirit carry also frontline?
Yes. Some ability builds have the durability and close-range pressure to take space. That still requires a survivable commitment and teammates who can use the opening.

role-support.title: How to Play Support in Deadlock | Deadlock Item Builder
role-support.meta: Learn Deadlock support fundamentals: save timing, positioning, farm priority, lane pressure, team utility and choosing counter items that help teammates.
blocks: How to Play Support in Deadlock
Keep your team able to act. Support impact comes from timely saves, useful control, efficient resources and a position that lets you affect the next important exchange.
Know who needs your next spell
Stay in reach without sharing a catch

Your job is to improve your teammates’ ability to fight. Healing, barriers, repositioning, buffs and control can all do that. Support is not limited to healing, and a damage spell can still create utility by making an enemy approach expensive.

You often need less farm to deliver your core utility than a dedicated carry, but useful items and survival still matter. A support who dies before the save or spends every spell on an irrelevant trade cannot protect the teammate the fight depends on.
Heroes that can play this role

Violet enables teammates through route control, improved allied sliding and an ultimate area that grants Spirit Power. Her utility depends on placement and follow-up; this role does not imply she provides every kind of heal or save.
These are common playstyles, not exclusive classes. Your build and team needs decide which job to emphasise.
See how builds change these heroes’ jobs

Help secure souls while making the opponent’s trades uncomfortable. Use cover, pressure and utility to keep your partner able to collect the wave. Avoid taking damage that forces both of you to retreat when a better angle would have delivered the same value.

Watch both your partner’s health and the enemy’s commitment. A barrier or heal used too early may expire before the real threat, while waiting too long can leave no activation window. Coordinate control with your partner’s follow-up rather than casting simply because the spell is ready.
For the shared fundamentals, read the [Deadlock laning guide](/guides/laning-counterplay).

Collect accessible resources between meaningful movements. You do not need to stand beside a farming carry while nothing threatens them. Cover another wave, take a safe resource route or move with a teammate who can turn your utility into pressure.

Avoid competing for the same resources when a teammate is close to an important spike and another useful route is open. Lower farm priority should make the team more efficient; it should not turn you into a player who never buys items or leaves waves undefended.

Move toward the teammate or objective most likely to need your next spell. A frontline entering contested ground may need immediate help, while a carry farming safely may not. Check visibility and travel time so the intended save is still possible when you arrive.

Stand where you can reach an important ally without sharing every enemy catch with them. Use cover and keep a route out. If you are the team’s main save, remaining alive can matter more than adding a small amount of damage from an exposed position.

Track the threat your utility is meant to answer. Hold a save for a dangerous catch when that is the deciding problem, but avoid sitting on every cooldown while allies lose a winnable fight. Help them survive long enough to use their own damage or escape.

Change priorities as the fight develops. Protect the ally currently able to win the exchange, interrupt a diver, or help finish an exposed threat. Supporting the team does not mean following one designated carry regardless of what is happening.
How to choose items for your role

Buy utility you can use from your actual position. A [Rescue Beam](/counter-items/rescue-beam) purchase needs a reachable ally and safe timing; another active may be a better fit if your hero cannot consistently deliver the save. Personal durability can be the strongest team purchase when dying is what prevents your utility.

Coordinate anti-heal, control and other targeted counters with teammates. Select application that fits your kit, and use the [item stacking guide](/guides/counter-items-stacking) before assuming duplicates add equal value. Protect your own activation window with the right [control defense](/guides/crowd-control) if you are repeatedly caught first.
Use the [Counter Item Helper](/counter-item-helper) to compare answers to the enemy heroes, then choose the purchase that fits your job.
Standing on top of the ally you want to save and being caught with them.
Giving up all farm, then lacking the items needed for the next fight.
Using a save on minor poke just before the enemy’s real commitment.
Following one ally all game while the rest of the team needs your utility elsewhere.

On Rem, identify who is about to receive focused pressure and keep a safe route to support them. If no one is threatened, collect accessible resources or help a rotation rather than waiting beside a carry who is already safe.
[Back to the full hero roles chart →](/roles)
No. Barriers, control, buffs, displacement and saves can all support teammates. The role is defined by the value you enable, not by having a healing spell.
No. Collect resources that keep your items progressing without needlessly competing with a higher-priority teammate for the same safe farm. Covering an unattended wave can help both you and the team.
Can you have impact on support in solo queue?
Yes. Timely saves, protecting a strong teammate and coordinating reliable control can change fights. Focus on useful actions you can deliver even when communication is limited.

comp-lockdown.title: How to Counter CC-Heavy Teams in Deadlock | Deadlock Item Builder
comp-lockdown.meta: Separate preventing a catch from surviving its follow-up. Spread the engage, track the control chain, and keep the right response available before it lands.
blocks: How to Counter CC-Heavy Teams in Deadlock
Separate preventing a catch from surviving its follow-up. Spread the engage, track the control chain, and keep the right response available before it lands.

Identify the first catch and the damage that follows it. Use proactive protection for a planned commitment, a cleanse only for effects it can remove, or passive defense and ally saves when you cannot act in time.
Best counter items against heavy cc teams
Choose it when repeated debuffs reduce the time you can move, cast or fight.
It is passive protection, not a cleanse. Check the exact effect rather than expecting every displacement to disappear.
Choose it when you can anticipate the control during an important cast or engage.
Activate before the catch. It is not a rescue button you can assume will work after all actions are disabled.
Choose it when a removable setup effect is causing the next lethal sequence.
Use it only when you have an activation window and the effect is eligible; do not treat it as an answer to every ultimate.
Choose it when control connects and immediate follow-up damage is the reason you die.
Use the resulting survival window to move or receive help. The item does not cancel the original control.
Choose it when you can hold a safe angle and reach the caught teammate.
Avoid sharing the same area catch. A save is useful only if the rescuer remains able to act.
Choose the item that answers the recurring threat and fits your hero. These are situational options, not a five-item shopping list.
Know which spell starts the lethal sequence.
Reposition when their key control is spent.
How to recognise this team style

Look for repeated fights where one stun, root, silence or displacement reliably leads to more control and focused damage. The decisive issue is losing your response window, not just facing many heroes with a disable.
Silence, stun, disarm and item denial are different problems. Read the effect that actually catches you, including whether it prevents the active item you intend to use.
Do not give one area spell access to your carry and the teammate responsible for saving them. Hold separate angles within useful range, and keep cover between you and a targeted catch.

Know the first enemy setup before starting an important cast. If your plan requires proactive immunity, activate it for that commitment; waiting until you are already disabled can remove the action window you needed.
After an enemy misses or spends the first catch, move into a better angle while it is unavailable. Avoid returning to the same exposed spot and letting the next cycle begin on their terms.

Call the difference between surviving the control and removing it. A barrier may keep the victim alive, while an ally needs to interrupt the follow-up or finish an exposed attacker. If an ultimate cannot be interrupted in that state, switch to leaving the area or saving its target.
Heroes that can contribute to this style

Violet adds a completion stun through Still Life and silence and slow when enemies leave Abstract Landscape. Respect those different timings; do not assume one cleanse answers every part of the setup.

These are examples of the threat, not a fixed draft recipe. Builds and team decisions change the way these heroes contribute. For split-push especially, look at the map behaviour rather than treating the tag as a permanent hero role.
Assuming every disable can be cleansed.
Holding proactive immunity until you are unable to activate it.
Letting the save hero get caught in the same area as the intended target.

Dive teams Enemies close distance to overwhelm a carry or support before the team can respond. See items & game plan →
How to Counter Poke Comps in Deadlock
Poke teams Enemies wear you down from range and control open approaches. See items & game plan →
How to Counter Healing and Sustain Comps in Deadlock
Sustain teams Enemies extend fights through healing, recovery, barriers and saves. See items & game plan →
How to Counter Burst Comps in Deadlock
Burst teams Enemies concentrate damage into a short combo or catch-and-finish window. See items & game plan →
How to Counter Split-Push Teams in Deadlock
Split-Push teams Enemies pressure side lanes while your team is occupied elsewhere. See items & game plan →
What is the best counter to crowd control in Deadlock?
There is no universal item answer. Identify whether you need prevention, an eligible cleanse, passive status resistance, protection from follow-up damage or an ally save.
Does Dispel Magic remove all crowd control?
No. This guide uses it for eligible removable non-ultimate debuffs, and only when you can activate it. Check the exact effect instead of assuming every catch or ultimate is removable.
Before a predictable control window during a commitment you need to complete. Do not assume you can wait until a stun has already removed your ability to act.

comp-split-push.title: How to Counter Split-Push Teams in Deadlock | Deadlock Item Builder
comp-split-push.meta: Keep waves covered, track the missing pusher, and send enough help to protect the objective without giving away the rest of the map.
blocks: How to Counter Split-Push Teams in Deadlock
Keep waves covered, track the missing pusher, and send enough help to protect the objective without giving away the rest of the map.
Wave coverage and timely rotations come first. Clear the immediate pressure, account for the pusher’s escape, and avoid sending the whole team after one enemy while another objective is exposed.
Best counter items against split-push teams
Choose it when a smaller wave- or summon-clear purchase lets you protect the lane without delaying the rest of your build.
Use the improved clear from a safe angle; it does not make an unsupported duel against the pusher safe.
Choose it when your weapon build can use a larger investment against waves or summons as well as in fights.
Buy for repeated value across your build. Do not rush a large purchase solely because one wave is at an objective.
Choose it when the pusher survives rotations through a movement ability this item can disable.
Apply before the escape, then follow with damage from teammates who can reach the target.
Choose it when a cast repeatedly defeats your coordinated catch.
Use before the cast and respect protection or cleanse tools. It is not a map-coverage solution by itself.
Choose it when your group can cover the delay and finish the pusher after the stun.
Check the target’s protection and keep damage in reach; a warning over their head does not guarantee a kill.
Choose the item that answers the recurring threat and fits your hero. These are situational options, not a five-item shopping list.
Respond before the objective is overwhelmed.
Know what a missing enemy can pressure.
Send enough help, then reassess the map.
How to recognise this team style
Split-push is a map decision rather than a fixed hero class. Look for someone repeatedly taking a side wave or objective while the rest of their team occupies your attention elsewhere.
A fast clearer or mobile hero can support that plan, but hero selection alone does not prove the enemy is split-pushing. Read the wave state, visibility and objective pressure.

Assign a player who can clear the immediate pressure without taking a losing duel. If they need help, make the rotation explicit and check which other lane or objective becomes vulnerable when that help leaves.

Move early enough to protect the objective. Arriving after the pusher has already cleared the wave and escaped may gain little. Keep nearby routes covered where practical, while accounting for enemies missing from the rest of the map.
Use a coordinated catch when the pusher’s position and escape route are known. Do not over-rotate all available players unless the reward justifies what you give up elsewhere.

If the enemy pusher remains far away and your team has a strong local advantage, a useful objective commitment may be better than a long chase. Reassess the trade: what can they take, what can you secure, and how safely can your defender hold?
Heroes that can contribute to this style

These are examples of the threat, not a fixed draft recipe. Builds and team decisions change the way these heroes contribute. For split-push especially, look at the map behaviour rather than treating the tag as a permanent hero role.
Buying a counter active while leaving the wave uncovered.
Sending the whole team to chase one pusher.
Choosing a defender who cannot clear or survive the matchup.
How to Counter Dive Comps in Deadlock
Dive teams Enemies close distance to overwhelm a carry or support before the team can respond. See items & game plan →
How to Counter Poke Comps in Deadlock
Poke teams Enemies wear you down from range and control open approaches. See items & game plan →
How to Counter CC-Heavy Teams in Deadlock
Heavy CC teams Enemies chain stuns, roots, silence or displacement to deny your response. See items & game plan →
How to Counter Healing and Sustain Comps in Deadlock
Sustain teams Enemies extend fights through healing, recovery, barriers and saves. See items & game plan →
How to Counter Burst Comps in Deadlock
Burst teams Enemies concentrate damage into a short combo or catch-and-finish window. See items & game plan →
What is the best counter to split-push in Deadlock?
Cover waves early, choose a defender who can clear safely and rotate only the help needed. Items support the plan, but do not replace map coverage.
Should everyone rotate to a split-pusher?
Usually send enough help for the actual threat and check what you give up elsewhere. Over-rotating can let the rest of the enemy team take another objective.
Does a mobile hero always count as split-push?
No. Split-push describes repeated side-lane pressure while teammates occupy another area. Tag the strategy you observe rather than assuming every mobile hero plays it.

guide-shielding-vs-resistance.title: Deadlock Shielding vs Resistance: Which Should You Buy?
guide-shielding-vs-resistance.meta: Compare shielding and resistance in Deadlock. Learn how barrier triggers, health pools and damage types affect Spirit Shielding, Weapon Shielding and resistance buys.
blocks: Deadlock Shielding vs Resistance: Which Should You Buy?
By Deadlock Item Builder · Practical matchup guide

Shielding adds a temporary damage buffer. Resistance reduces incoming damage of the relevant type. The better purchase depends on how a fight starts, how long you stay exposed and whether your hero can use the protection to keep contributing.

Choose a shielding item when its trigger reliably creates a useful survival window. Compare resistance when the same damage type keeps hurting you across repeated exchanges. A barrier and resistance can work together; neither replaces movement or control defense.
Choose for the problem you are facing; these are alternatives to compare, not a full shopping list.
An ability burst starts a trade you cannot survive.
The spirit-damage trigger reliably creates a barrier before the follow-up kills you.
The barrier comes after the trigger; it does not prevent the opening cast or remove its control.
Gunfire starts the enemy’s winning trade.
Weapon pressure reliably triggers a barrier you can use to reach cover or trade back.
The weapon trigger must occur. The resulting barrier can absorb other damage too.
Spirit damage wears you down through repeated exchanges.
You need passive defense against recurring spirit damage while staying in the fight.
It does not remove debuffs or prevent control, and it is not a general answer to weapon damage.
A large spirit hit and debuff pressure decide the fight.
You need spirit defense and can keep its burst-protection effect ready for the important hit.
An earlier qualifying hit can spend its periodic protection before the big ability lands.
What is the difference between shielding and resistance?

A barrier is a temporary buffer that absorbs damage until it is spent or expires. Resistance reduces the damage you take of the relevant type. That means a barrier can give you immediate room to survive a trade, while resistance helps whenever that damage type reaches you.

Do not read Spirit Shielding and Weapon Shielding as two barriers that only absorb their named damage types. In the supplied itemization guide, the names describe their triggers: a burst of spirit damage or weapon damage creates the barrier. Once active, that barrier can absorb other incoming damage too.
When should you buy a shielding item?

Start with the opening exchange. If a spirit burst reliably begins the enemy’s combo, Spirit Shielding is an option to compare. If gun pressure starts the losing trade, investigate Weapon Shielding. If a hard-control catch is the trigger, Reactive Barrier solves a different opening pattern.

The useful question is what you do after the shield appears. Reach cover, reset the angle or return damage your team can follow up on. A barrier is less valuable if its trigger never happens in the matchup or the enemy can keep attacking after it is gone.
When should you buy resistance instead?

Resistance is worth comparing when you repeatedly take the same damage type and need to remain present through several exchanges. Spirit Resilience offers a passive spirit-defense option; Spellbreaker adds another kind of protection against spirit burst. Check each item’s conditions rather than comparing only the headline resistance.

A larger health pool generally gives percentage damage reduction more health to protect. That helps explain why a durable frontliner and a fragile backline hero may choose differently against the same damage source. It is a comparison point, not a rule that every frontliner must buy resistance.
Can you combine shielding and resistance?

The supplied itemization guide describes barriers as benefiting from resistance, so these options can complement each other. That does not mean buying every defensive item is efficient. Check whether the next purchase meaningfully changes the fight or simply delays a core item you need to contribute.

Repeated resistance purchases also have diminishing combined value; do not add their percentages as if each applied independently to the original damage. Avoid publishing a universal effective-health calculation without accounting for the current item effects, enemy resistance shred and the actual damage mix.
Choose defense for the next fight, not the hero name

Ask three questions: what damage is killing you, what triggers the item, and what action its protection enables. If the enemy’s control stops you using your abilities, a larger barrier or more resistance may leave that problem unchanged. If their damage has shifted to weapons, a spirit-defense purchase may miss the new threat.

You do not always need to tank the exchange. A different angle, an escape or a well-timed defensive active may preserve more of your damage budget. Compare those alternatives when the fight is decided by a single commitment rather than sustained exposure.
How to choose in real matchups
Grey Talon opens the trade with a spirit hit
Compare Spirit Shielding when his ability burst reliably triggers it. Use the barrier window to take hard cover before the next shot; the purchase does not justify staying in the same exposed angle.
Drifter follows a catch with weapon pressure
Weapon Shielding may help absorb the gun follow-up. A shield is a separate answer from removing the mark that enables his approach; decide which part of the sequence is actually costing the fight.
Assuming a shield only absorbs the damage type in the item’s name.
Choosing a barrier whose trigger does not occur in the matchup.
Adding resistance percentages directly or ignoring enemy resistance shred.
Does Spirit Shielding only block spirit damage?
The spirit damage is its trigger. The resulting barrier can absorb other incoming damage as well, while it remains available.
Is shielding better than resistance in Deadlock?
Neither is always better. Compare a triggered survival window with ongoing reduction against the damage type you actually face, then account for your health pool, role and core build.

comp-sustain.title: How to Counter Healing and Sustain Comps in Deadlock | Deadlock Item Builder
comp-sustain.meta: Stop giving recovery free value. Apply healing reduction before focused damage, track saves, and change targets when protection makes the finish unrealistic.
blocks: How to Counter Healing and Sustain Comps in Deadlock
Stop giving recovery free value. Apply healing reduction before focused damage, track saves, and change targets when protection makes the finish unrealistic.

Use anti-heal when recovery keeps an enemy alive, and apply it before your team commits damage. Against barriers or saves, bait protection or switch targets; healing reduction alone does not answer those effects.
Best counter items against sustain teams
Choose it when your build can repeatedly hit the relevant target with spirit damage.
Apply before focused damage and maintain access to the target. Reliable application matters more than simply owning the item.
Choose it when sustained weapon contact fits your normal job in the fight.
Build the effect on the target your team intends to finish; do not spread all damage while the healer recovers each trade.
Choose it when direct application gives your team a clearer finish opportunity.
Coordinate the damage during that window. The target still needs to be reachable and vulnerable.
Choose it when a castable save or escape repeatedly defeats your team’s commitment.
Time it before the defensive cast; it does not remove a barrier that is already protecting the target.
Choose it when a large health pool is the remaining problem after healing or saves are addressed.
Do not confuse health damage with healing reduction. It complements the finish plan instead of replacing anti-heal.
Choose the item that answers the recurring threat and fits your hero. These are situational options, not a five-item shopping list.
Separate healing from barriers and saves.
Apply anti-heal or force a defensive cooldown.
Focus during the window you created.
How to recognise this team style

Healing and recovery let enemies erase small damage commitments. Teamwide saves or barriers can produce a similar-looking problem, but they need a different response. Look at what restores health and what prevents the damage from landing.

An enemy with sustain is not automatically the best target. If a durable frontline cannot be finished, hitting it repeatedly may only use your cooldowns while a protected damage dealer wins the fight.
Avoid a long exchange inside the area where the enemy team has its strongest recovery or protection. Change the angle or move the fight so the save hero must expose themselves to keep helping.
Use short pressure to force a defensive response, then choose whether to wait it out or change targets. Do not stand in the same unfavourable space spending every spell into protection.

Apply healing reduction before the damage you need to convert into a kill. Coordinate the target so enough damage arrives during the same window. If a save is still available, account for it before treating the low health bar as a guaranteed finish.

Pressure an exposed healer when your team can reach them, but avoid a solo chase through the frontline. If you cannot reach the healer, force a save, switch to a vulnerable target or disengage until a better commitment is available.
Heroes that can contribute to this style

These are examples of the threat, not a fixed draft recipe. Builds and team decisions change the way these heroes contribute. For split-push especially, look at the map behaviour rather than treating the tag as a permanent hero role.
Applying anti-heal after the enemy has already recovered.
Treating barriers as healing and expecting anti-heal to remove them.
Spreading chip damage across several targets instead of coordinating a finish.

What items counter healing teams in Deadlock?
Healbane, Toxic Bullets and Decay offer different ways to apply healing reduction. Choose the one your hero can use reliably on the target your team intends to finish.
Anti-heal addresses healing and recovery; do not assume it removes a barrier. Bait the protection, change targets or deny the defensive cast before it happens.
Should you always focus the healer first?
Only when the healer is reachable and the team can follow. Otherwise, force their save or focus another exposed target during a coordinated healing-reduction window.

guide-mobility.title: Deadlock Mobility Counters: Slowing Hex vs Knockdown
guide-mobility.meta: Counter mobile Deadlock heroes with Slowing Hex, Knockdown and Silence Wave. Compare escape control, flying targets, timing and follow-up against cleanses.
blocks: Deadlock Mobility Counters: Slowing Hex vs Knockdown
By Deadlock Item Builder · Practical matchup guide
A movement ability, a flying angle and a defensive cast are different ways to escape. Choose control that addresses the actual tool, then time it so your team can finish the catch.
Control the escape before committing damage, and plan around cleanses and immunity.
Slowing Hex vs Knockdown vs Silence Wave
Start with the problem you need to solve. These are situational choices, not a list to buy in full.
The enemy uses a movement ability to escape before your team can finish them.
The target relies on an affected movement ability and your team can attack before the control ends.
Check the hero’s ability interaction. A cleanse or an escape used before your cast can spoil the catch.
The enemy stays airborne or channels an ability your team needs to interrupt.
You need delayed control against an airborne target or an interruptible channel, with follow-up ready.
The stun is delayed. Check for a cleanse, immunity or another defensive response before relying on it.
The enemy’s ability casts let them survive or escape your team’s attack.
You can land the silence before a key escape or defensive cast, while your team is ready to attack.
Silence alone is not a reliable interrupt for an already-running channel. Land it before the important cast.
Identify the escape they are saving

Mobile heroes often survive because they keep one tool for the moment your team commits. Watch whether they escape with a movement ability, a defensive cast, height, or ordinary stamina. These demand different answers. A movement-focused item should not be assumed to disable every ability that changes position.

Pocket, Lash and Calico are useful examples to study in the hero guides. Look for what they hold until they are threatened and what they spend to enter the fight. An escape already on cooldown may be a better opportunity than a new item purchase.
Use Slowing Hex before the escape

Slowing Hex is a candidate when a movement ability is keeping the target safe. Apply it when your team can follow up and before the escape you want to stop. Using control on a distant opponent while your damage dealers cannot reach them often gives the enemy time to wait it out.

Check the matchup rather than treating the item as a universal movement shutdown. The supplied guide notes that The Doorman’s door is not answered in the same way as a conventional movement ability. That distinction matters more than the hero appearing to move quickly.
Choose Knockdown or silence for a different job

Knockdown is useful to compare when height or an interruptible channel is the real problem. Its delay means your team still needs to track the target and be ready to act when it lands. Vindicta and Grey Talon are obvious places to consult the dedicated matchup advice.

Silence Wave targets ability access rather than only movement. It can help create a kill window against an ability-dependent target, but requires appropriate positioning and follow-up. The more expensive answer is only worth saving for when it solves the threat you are actually facing.
Plan a second layer when the first is answered

Inspect the enemy’s defensive items. If a cleanse keeps removing your control, coordinate a second application or hold another effect for after the cleanse. Two teammates casting at the same instant can waste the window that a staggered sequence would create.

Keep enough movement to follow a reachable target, but avoid turning a failed catch into a long chase away from objectives. A useful counter also creates space: forcing an escape or a defensive cooldown can let your team take a better fight even when the target survives.
How to use these counters in real matchups
Pocket holds an escape for your commitment
Study which escape option remains available. Apply the relevant control before the exit you want to deny, and have someone ready to cover the alternate position.
The Doorman uses a door to reposition
The supplied counterbuying guide distinguishes his door from conventional movement abilities. Check the matchup rather than assuming Slowing Hex disables anything that moves a hero.
Casting control when teammates are too far away.
Layering every effect into one enemy cleanse.
Chasing so far that a failed catch costs the objective.
Does Slowing Hex stop every escape in Deadlock?
No. Its value depends on the ability interaction. Look up the specific hero and distinguish movement abilities from other ways to reposition or survive.
When should your team use a second control item?
When a cleanse, immunity window or alternate escape defeats the first layer, stagger follow-up deliberately. Two instant casts can waste what a sequenced catch would achieve.

guide-channeled-ultimates.title: How to Stop Channeled Ultimates in Deadlock
guide-channeled-ultimates.meta: Compare Knockdown, silence and stuns against Deadlock channeled ultimates. Learn interrupt timing, immunity checks and what to do when a channel cannot be stopped.
blocks: How to Stop Channeled Ultimates in Deadlock
By Deadlock Item Builder · Practical matchup guide
Knockdown, silence and a stun are different tools. The right answer depends on whether the ultimate has started, how long you have to react and whether the enemy is protected from control.

Use a stun to interrupt a channel that is vulnerable to control. [Knockdown](/counter-items/knockdown) supplies a delayed stun; silence is more dependable for denying the cast before it begins. If immunity protects the channel, switch to cover, distance or an ally save.
Choose an answer for the current casting window
Interrupt a vulnerable channel or punish an exposed airborne caster
Cast early enough for the delayed stun to land
The effect can be denied by a cleanse or control immunity
Deny a new ultimate, escape or defensive cast
Land before the cast with allied damage ready
Does not universally cancel an already-running channel
Range, availability and control immunity still matter
Create a coordinated ability, weapon and item-denial window
Use while the target is vulnerable and allies can follow
Not a guaranteed interrupt through immunity
Reduce the value of a protected channel
Move or rescue before the follow-up becomes lethal
Does not mean the channel itself was canceled
Knockdown vs silence vs stun: which one stops the channel?

Start with the channel’s current state. Before the cast, silence can deny an important ability and create a finish window. Once a channel is running, you need an effect that actually interrupts that ability. A silence is not a universal cancellation button for every active ultimate.

[Knockdown](/counter-items/knockdown) is an interrupt because its delayed effect is a stun, not because the cast immediately shuts the target down. A hero’s ready instant stun can be the better response when the channel is short or the damage has already put someone close to death.

Cast [Knockdown](/counter-items/knockdown) early during an exposed channel, then plan for the delay before the stun arrives. If you wait until the victim is nearly dead, the ultimate can finish its job before the control lands. Call the target so allies know when to move, interrupt again or deal follow-up damage.

Seven’s Storm Cloud, Bebop’s Hyper Beam, Haze’s Bullet Dance and McGinnis’s Heavy Barrage are practical examples of channels where a vulnerable caster can be interrupted. Check the target’s active protection instead of assuming that buying [Knockdown](/counter-items/knockdown) guarantees the same result every fight.

Avoid spending several delayed interrupts at once unless you need that overlap. A cleanse can remove a pending effect, while control immunity can deny the stun. Keeping a second response for after the defensive window is often more useful than losing every answer to the same protection.
When silence is the better purchase

Choose [Silence Wave](/counter-items/silence-wave) when denying the next cast would let your team finish the target. Land it while allies are ready to commit. That is a stronger reason to buy silence than hoping it will cancel a channel you have not checked.

The same timing distinction matters outside channeled ultimates. Silence before Kelvin casts Frozen Shelter or Yamato activates Shadow Transformation can deny the defensive response. A late silence does not erase an existing dome or transformation. Stopping a future cast and removing an active effect are different jobs.
What if the enemy uses Unstoppable?

An active [Unstoppable](/counter-items/unstoppable) window can stop the control your interrupt depends on. Read that protection before committing [Knockdown](/counter-items/knockdown) or another disable. Do not keep standing in the damage area because you expect the next control cast to override immunity.

Against a protected Storm Cloud or Hyper Beam, break the damaging line of sight. Against Dynamo’s protected Singularity, keep rescuers outside the catch and consider [Rescue Beam](/counter-items/rescue-beam) for a trapped ally. Your goal becomes reducing the ultimate’s value rather than insisting on a cancel that is unavailable.

Survival items still have their own limits. [Metal Skin](/counter-items/metal-skin) can protect a committed bullet-damage window such as Haze’s weapon ultimate pressure; it is not a spirit-damage defense for Heavy Barrage. Match the fallback to the actual damage source.
Make the interrupt part of a team plan

Before an objective fight, decide who holds the first interrupt and who can act if it is denied. A support outside the damage area may have a better activation window than the player being caught. An unused instant stun is worth more than a second delayed item cast after the victim has already died.

Follow the successful interrupt with damage or a safer position. Canceling a channel without a follow-up plan may only buy the opponent time to retreat. After the enemy adds immunity, update the plan: bait it, wait out the window, reposition or save the threatened teammate.
Use the answer in a real matchup

Use [Knockdown](/counter-items/knockdown) while the channel is vulnerable. When Seven has active [Unstoppable](/counter-items/unstoppable), break the sight line instead of feeding more damage attempts into the same exposed position.

Interrupt an exposed McGinnis early and account for the delayed stun. If control protection denies the stop, use cover and a safe reposition; bullet immunity does not answer this spirit-damage channel.
Keep a teammate outside the catch able to rescue or respond. A protected channel changes the plan from forcing a cancel to moving allies toward safety and avoiding another grouped engage.
Casting Knockdown too late for its stun to matter.
Treating silence as a universal active-ultimate cancel.
Ignoring Unstoppable or a pending-effect cleanse.
Using bullet protection against a spirit-damage channel.
Does silence cancel all channeled ultimates in Deadlock?

No. Silence is useful for denying a cast before it happens, but it is not a universal cancel for every running ultimate. Use an interrupt that works on the specific vulnerable channel, and check whether active control immunity prevents that response.
Is Knockdown better than an instant stun?

[Knockdown](/counter-items/knockdown) is useful when your team lacks a reliable stop or needs access to an exposed caster. Its stun is delayed, so a ready instant hero stun can be better when the channel is short or someone needs an immediate save. Both still depend on control vulnerability.
What should you do if Unstoppable blocks your interrupt?

Switch to the available survival plan: break the damage angle, leave the area or rescue a trapped teammate. Keep another response for after immunity ends rather than spending every disable into the same protection. The safest fallback depends on the ultimate and its damage source.

guide-gun-damage.meta: Compare Metal Skin, Plated Armor, Disarming Hex and Suppressor to counter gun damage in Deadlock. Match your purchase to burst windows and sustained pressure.
blocks: Deadlock Gun Counters: Metal Skin vs Plated Armor
By Deadlock Item Builder · Practical matchup guide

Gun damage counters serve different jobs: survive a dangerous window, reduce repeated weapon pressure, or interrupt the shooter. Compare those jobs before deciding whether Metal Skin, Plated Armor or a disruption item fits your next fight.
Compare a short defensive window, sustained protection and a disarm; use cover to limit follow-up.
Which item should you buy against gun damage?
Start with the problem you need to solve. These are situational choices, not a list to buy in full.
A burst of enemy gunfire kills you before you can reposition.
You need a short window to survive weapon damage and reach cover or finish a committed fight.
Ability damage and control can still threaten you. Have a plan for when the active expires.
Repeated gunfire wears you down throughout fights.
You face repeated weapon hits and want passive protection against bullet and on-hit pressure.
Its protection is chance-based, not guaranteed immunity. It does not remove stacks already applied.
An enemy carry keeps shooting freely during your team’s engage.
You can reach a weapon-focused carry and your team can attack while their gun is disabled.
A cleanse can remove the disarm. It does not shut down all of the target’s ability damage.
An enemy’s rapid gunfire makes it difficult for your team to trade damage.
Your hero can consistently apply spirit damage to the gun carry you want to slow down.
Reduced fire rate is not a full disarm; the enemy can still shoot and use abilities.

A hero firing a gun is not proof that all their threatening damage is weapon damage. On-hit effects and ability investment can change what you need to survive. Inspect the build and the damage that ended the fight before choosing protection. Haze, Wraith and Drifter can all demand attention, but the answer depends on what that player is doing.

Baba is a useful reminder to check the details: the supplied guide describes spirit damage attached to her shots through Thread Sap. A purchase aimed only at weapon damage should not be treated as a complete answer to that pressure.
Use Metal Skin to change a short window

Metal Skin provides a temporary answer to weapon pressure. Plan what you will do with that time: cross an exposed angle, get out of an ultimate’s danger, reach cover, or stay alive while your team finishes a target. Activating it and remaining in the same losing position can simply delay the problem until it expires.

It is a defensive window rather than permission to ignore the rest of the enemy team. Ability damage and control may still force you out. If you cannot act when the threat arrives, you may need an answer to the setup as well.

Plated Armor is worth comparing when repeated weapon pressure is the recurring problem. Disarming Hex approaches the fight from the other side: interrupt the attacker’s weapon output so your team can act. Suppressor can also fit spirit-damage users who can consistently reach the gun carry.

Choose based on access. A defensive item can help when the carry attacks you from an angle you cannot contest. A targeted disruption item needs a usable range and a moment to cast it. If you cannot reach the attacker safely, do not build a plan around a cast you never get to make.
Break the angle and punish commitment

Use corners and cover to reduce uninterrupted shooting time. Avoid crossing an open lane after spending all your stamina. A carry who commits into your defensive window should face your teammates’ return damage; a carry holding a distant angle may be better handled by a rotation.

Watch their next purchase. A cleanse or another defensive tool can change how reliable your disruption is. Agree on follow-up with your team and reassess after fights. If you survived but dealt no useful damage, review whether too much of your build went into protection at once.
How to use these counters in real matchups
Haze forces you out during her damage window
Compare a short defensive active with sustained protection. Decide where you will move and who follows up while you survive; waiting in the same exposed spot can leave the next burst unanswered.

Thread Sap is described in the supplied guide as adding spirit damage to her shots. A gun-defense purchase should not be treated as a complete answer to that build; check the damage source and the Baba matchup guide.
Assuming all damage from gunfire is weapon damage.
Activating Metal Skin without an escape or follow-up plan.
Buying a targeted disarm when you cannot reach the attacker.
Is Metal Skin or Plated Armor better against gun damage?

Compare the fight pattern. Metal Skin provides a temporary defensive window; Plated Armor is an option to investigate for repeated weapon pressure. Your hero, the damage source and the enemy build decide the fit.
Does Metal Skin solve crowd control too?
A weapon-defense window is not a blanket answer to disables. If control prevents you from using your items, investigate the setup separately.

guide-counter-silence.title: How to Counter Silence in Deadlock
guide-counter-silence.meta: Counter silence in Deadlock with eligible cleanses, debuff resistance, Unstoppable and better positioning. Learn how silence differs from stun, disarm and item denial.
blocks: How to Counter Silence in Deadlock
By Deadlock Item Builder · Practical matchup guide

A silence can stop the defensive cast or escape you were saving, but it is not the same as a stun or item lock. Choose the response for the actual effect, then use the action window to reach a position you can survive.

Use [Dispel Magic](/counter-items/dispel-magic) for an eligible non-ultimate silence when item activation remains available. [Debuff Reducer](/counter-items/debuff-reducer) shortens negative-effect duration, while [Unstoppable](/counter-items/unstoppable) protects a planned commitment when activated in time. If item denial or a stun is also present, an active cleanse may not be available.
Choose a silence response for the action window you have
An eligible non-ultimate silence or debuff
You can activate before the follow-up becomes lethal
Excludes ultimate debuffs; item denial can prevent activation
Shorter duration creates a real retreat or trade window
Does not cleanse, prevent application or absorb damage
Control that would stop a planned commitment
You can protect the important window before the catch
Cannot be activated while stunned or slept; no damage immunity
A readable incoming ability in the relevant matchup
You can time the spell parry for the decisive hit
Not a general removal tool for silence already applied
A pick you cannot answer from inside the catch
You can deny access or keep a helper outside the angle
Needs a safer route and coordinated follow-up

Ordinary silence restricts ability casting. It is different from a stun or sleep that removes your action window, a disarm that stops weapon attacks, or an effect that blocks active items. A combination of those effects can feel like one long shutdown, but the distinction determines which response you can still use.

[Silence Wave](/counter-items/silence-wave) is a cast-denial tool, while [Silencer](/counter-items/silencer) needs weapon buildup to reach its silence. [Slowing Hex](/counter-items/slowing-hex) restricts affected movement abilities rather than acting as a full silence for every cast. Cursed Relic combines several restrictions, including item denial, so it should not be treated as ordinary silence alone.

[Dispel Magic](/counter-items/dispel-magic) is useful against eligible non-ultimate silence, including the removable [Silence Wave](/counter-items/silence-wave) effect discussed in the item guides. Use it while you can still activate an item, then leave the angle that made the next enemy hit easy. A cleanse restores an opportunity to respond; it does not absorb the follow-up damage.

Do not extend that rule to every ultimate effect. [Dispel Magic](/counter-items/dispel-magic) excludes ultimate debuffs. [Divine Barrier](/counter-items/divine-barrier) has a separate eligible removal role, but it is not a claim that every hard-control effect can be cleansed. Identify the source rather than buying a cleanse for the word “silence” alone.

If [Cursed Relic](/counter-items/cursed-relic)’s item denial is already active, do not plan on pressing a self-cleanse that the effect prevents you using. Avoid the pick before it lands, prepare protection, or keep a teammate safely positioned to help when your own actions are restricted.
When is Debuff Reducer useful against silence?

Choose [Debuff Reducer](/counter-items/debuff-reducer) when spending less time under negative effects would let you retreat or complete the next trade. It is passive, so its value does not depend on finding another active button during every exchange. It shortens the effect rather than preventing application or removing it outright.

A shorter silence can still be lethal if the enemy has already secured a point-blank damage window. If you die before the duration difference matters, prioritize preventing that catch, changing the angle or surviving the follow-up. Duration reduction is not a substitute for damage protection.
Use Unstoppable for a planned commitment

[Unstoppable](/counter-items/unstoppable) fits an engage or damage window that would fail if silence or other control denied your casts. Activate before the dangerous sequence so the protection covers the moment you actually commit. Using it too early lets the opponent wait; planning to use it after a stun or sleep lands can leave no activation window.

The item temporarily suppresses negative effects and protects against control during its active window. It does not grant damage immunity. Keep a route or a team response that survives the damage while your abilities remain available.
Avoid the silence window you cannot survive

Do not save every escape until you are already beside a cast-denial enemy. Use cover, preserve spacing and make the opponent commit the silence before your decisive entry when possible. Against weapon-applied [Silencer](/counter-items/silencer), short trades and breaking target access can deny the uninterrupted buildup it wants.

A readable incoming ability can also justify [Counterspell](/counter-items/counterspell) when the matchup supports that timing. Apollo’s ultimate is an example where the spell parry can answer the damaging payoff even after the initial setup. That does not make Counterspell a general cleanse for an already-applied silence.

When the team expects a cast-denial pick, keep someone outside the same angle able to rescue or counter-engage. If every player stacks into one control window, personal items alone may not restore a useful response.
Use the answer in a real matchup
The setup lands before the ultimate damage

Save [Counterspell](/counter-items/counterspell) for Apollo’s actual damaging hit rather than activating at the earliest cue. A silence alone and a stun are different action restrictions; the ability response must fit the timing you still have.

[Dispel Magic](/counter-items/dispel-magic) can remove eligible Threadsap or Brew debuffs, then you should change angle or reach cover. It does not cleanse Baba’s ultimate transformation, so keep a separate Feed the Birds response.
Repeated control keeps you on dangerous squares

[Debuff Reducer](/counter-items/debuff-reducer) can shorten eligible negative effects, but you still need to leave Solomon’s prepared ground. If the opening disable denies every response, plan prevention rather than expecting duration reduction to make the damage harmless.
Calling silence, stun, disarm and item denial the same effect.
Assuming Dispel Magic removes every ultimate debuff.
Planning an active self-cleanse through an existing item lock.
Buying duration reduction when you die before the shorter duration matters.
Can you use items while silenced in Deadlock?

Ordinary silence is different from item denial, so do not assume it removes every active-item response. Stun, sleep or a separate item-lock effect can prevent the activation you need. Identify the combined effects on you before relying on an active cleanse or protection item.

No. [Debuff Reducer](/counter-items/debuff-reducer) shortens negative-effect duration rather than cleansing or preventing the effect. It is useful when a shorter window lets you move or fight back. If the silence enables lethal damage immediately, preventing the catch or surviving the follow-up may be more valuable.
Does Dispel Magic remove every silence?

No. [Dispel Magic](/counter-items/dispel-magic) is for eligible non-ultimate debuffs and requires an available item activation. It is useful against removable silence such as [Silence Wave](/counter-items/silence-wave), but does not remove ultimate debuffs or let you ignore an existing item lock. Check the source and timing of the effect.

guide-counter-items-stacking.title: Do Counter Items Stack in Deadlock?
guide-counter-items-stacking.meta: Learn which Deadlock counter effects stack, how anti-heal and resistance diminishing returns work, and when teammates should buy different items instead of duplicates.
blocks: Do Counter Items Stack in Deadlock?
By Deadlock Item Builder · Practical matchup guide

Some counter effects combine, some duplicate applications do not add together, and many defensive items simply solve different problems. Check the effect you are stacking before spending another slot on it.

Different anti-heal sources can combine with diminishing returns; duplicate applications of the same anti-heal source do not add their percentages. Resistance also has diminishing returns. Complementary defenses can still be useful because they answer different parts of a fight.
Common counter effects and how to think about stacking
Do not add their percentages directly
The same anti-heal source from two players
Duplicate applications do not add reduction percentages
Coverage is different from stronger reduction
Duplicate only when uptime or access justifies it
Additional sources can combine with diminishing returns
Protection still depends on damage type and conditions
Compare another defense with fixing the catch or escape
Different sources can combine; same-source rules vary
Some effects have explicit stacks or exceptions
Check the item and coordinate the relevant damage
A disarm plus personal bullet protection
One needs enemy access; the other protects the user
Use complementary responses during the weapon commitment
Counter-item stacking depends on the effect

There is no single rule that covers every counter item. “Stacking” can mean adding two healing-reduction sources, combining damage resistance, keeping the same debuff applied, or owning two items with different defensive jobs. Those are separate questions.

Start by naming the effect you need more of. If healing prevents a finish, compare anti-heal sources. If damage is killing you, compare protection against that damage type. If control denies your actions, another resistance item may improve survival without fixing the catch.

Different anti-heal sources can combine on the same target with diminishing returns. [Healbane](/counter-items/healbane) plus [Toxic Bullets](/counter-items/toxic-bullets) is a useful example of different application methods. Two players applying Healbane do not create the same additive benefit as bringing another distinct anti-heal source.

Do not add the displayed percentages as if each reduction removes the same original healing. Each additional source reduces the healing that remains. For illustration, two hypothetical 30% reductions leave 70% × 70% = 49% of the original healing, or 51% total reduction—not 60%. These numbers illustrate the calculation rather than quote current item stats.

That does not make a second buyer useless. Another player may apply the effect when the first is dead, out of range or unable to damage the target. Coverage and reliability are useful, even when the duplicate source does not add another reduction percentage.
Does bullet or spirit resistance stack?

Additional resistance sources can improve damage protection, but they have diminishing returns rather than a simple percentage sum. The next purchase reduces part of the damage you would still take. More resistance can help, but its value should be compared with another item that fixes the way you are losing the fight.

For example, [Spirit Resilience](/counter-items/spirit-resilience) can help against repeated spirit pressure while a timed [Counterspell](/counter-items/counterspell) answers one readable incoming hit. [Metal Skin](/counter-items/metal-skin) offers a short bullet-immunity window. Those effects are not all extra copies of the same resistance stat, so do not judge the combination by adding their descriptions together.

Different resistance-reduction sources can combine with diminishing returns, but do not assume repeated applications of one source all add together. Some effects have explicit stack rules. Read that item’s current description rather than transferring an anti-heal rule to every resistance-shred item.

[Bullet Resist Shredder](/counter-items/bullet-resist-shredder) also needs the right follow-up. Reducing a durable target’s bullet defenses does little for a team that cannot reach it or deliver weapon damage during the effect. Application and access matter as much as owning another source of shred.
When should teammates buy different counter items?

Diversify when a different source solves a missing job. Against healing, one reliable spirit application and one reliable weapon application may provide more useful coverage than several players copying a source they struggle to maintain. Keep the decisive damage coordinated while the effects are active.

Diversify defenses for the sequence too. A teammate’s [Disarming Hex](/counter-items/disarming-hex) can stop enemy gunfire while the threatened carry uses [Metal Skin](/counter-items/metal-skin) to survive the commitment. Those buys have different targets and activation windows; they are useful because of those roles, not because their percentages stack.

Before buying another counter, ask whether the first answer is already applied when it matters. If it is, your missing resource may be damage, target access or a response to a cleanse. Another copy of the same effect will not automatically repair those problems.
Use the answer in a real matchup

Coordinate distinct anti-heal applications while your team commits focused damage. The important window is when healing reduction and team damage are both present, not simply how many anti-heal items appear in inventories.
The team needs survival and a weapon stop

A threatened player can use [Metal Skin](/counter-items/metal-skin) while a safely positioned ally applies [Disarming Hex](/counter-items/disarming-hex). Keep a separate answer for existing Fixation pressure; complementary buys do not mean every debuff disappears.
Assuming duplicate application always means a stronger effect.
Buying more resistance without fixing the control catch.
Calling an illustrative calculation a current item-stat example.
Does Healbane stack with Toxic Bullets?

Yes, different anti-heal sources can combine with diminishing returns when both are applied. The resulting reduction is not the simple sum of the displayed percentages. Choose the source your hero can maintain and coordinate damage during the shared application window.
Do two Healbanes double the healing reduction?

No. Duplicate [Healbane](/counter-items/healbane) applications do not add another reduction percentage like a distinct anti-heal source. A second buyer can still help maintain coverage when the first cannot apply it. Decide whether reliable uptime or a different application method is what your team needs.
Is stacking counter items always a bad idea?

No. Complementary items can answer different problems, such as surviving enemy gunfire and stopping the enemy from shooting. The mistake is buying another overlapping effect without checking what still makes you lose: damage, control, access, healing or the opponent’s cleanse.

guide-anti-heal.title: Deadlock Anti-Heal Items: Healbane vs Toxic Bullets
guide-anti-heal.meta: Compare Deadlock anti-heal items including Healbane, Toxic Bullets and Decay. Learn which fits your damage pattern and when to apply healing reduction.
blocks: Deadlock Anti-Heal Items: Healbane vs Toxic Bullets
By Deadlock Item Builder · Practical matchup guide

Healbane, Toxic Bullets and Decay answer healing in different ways. Choose the anti-heal item your hero can apply consistently, then bring damage into the same window instead of letting the enemy recover between trades.
Choose anti-heal you can apply reliably, then focus damage during the healing window.
Healbane vs Toxic Bullets vs Decay
Start with the problem you need to solve. These are situational choices, not a list to buy in full.
The enemy’s healing prevents your team from finishing the kill.
Your hero can repeatedly deal spirit damage to the enemy who is healing.
Apply it before or during the healing window; it does little if your spirit damage never reaches that target.
A target keeps healing while you shoot them.
Your hero can land enough consecutive shots to build the effect on the healing target.
A target that quickly breaks line of sight may escape before you apply the anti-heal.
A priority target recovers too much health during your team’s focused attack.
You need targeted anti-heal without relying on repeated shots or spirit-damage hits.
Cast it before your team commits damage; applying it after the enemy recovers misses the useful window.
Check whether healing is really saving them

A target surviving on low health can mean several things: healing, a barrier, resistance, an escape, or damage arriving one player at a time. Watch what happens as their health drops. If they recover through your team’s damage, healing reduction deserves attention. If they barely lose health in the first place, your team may also need better focus or a different damage answer.

Abrams, Shiv, Kelvin and Rem are useful matchups to investigate, but the enemy’s actual purchases matter. Lifesteal can make healing a problem on a damage carry too. Do not reserve anti-heal only for heroes you think of as healers.
Match application to your damage pattern

Healbane is a natural option when your spirit damage can reliably reach the healing target. Toxic Bullets suits weapon users who can repeatedly land shots and build the effect. Decay offers a targeted active option. Compare their dedicated pages for the effect and matchup context before fitting one into your build.

The strongest-looking effect is not automatically the best purchase. If your hero cannot maintain shots on the target, a shooting-based answer may arrive too late. If your abilities barely touch that enemy, a spirit-applied effect may sit unused when your team needs it most.
Apply it before the recovery window

Anti-heal needs to be present while the enemy is trying to recover. Communicate the target, apply your effect, and bring follow-up damage into the same window. A low-health opponent is not necessarily a safe chase: following them into a healing zone or around a corner can split your team and give them time to reset.

Against a sustain-heavy frontline, aim to make each committed trade count. Repeated small exchanges that the enemy fully recovers from can cost you health and cooldowns without creating meaningful pressure.
Pair healing reduction with a finish

Healing reduction does not stop every defensive tool. If Lady Geist is threatening a health swap, respect her close-range threat and consider control or spacing as part of your plan. If Kelvin is sustaining teammates inside his dome, avoid walking into a favorable fight for him just because you bought anti-heal.

Coordinate coverage rather than assuming more anti-heal purchases always mean more value. A teammate who can maintain the effect may let you buy control or damage instead. When the enemy changes how they survive, revisit the helper and answer the new problem.
How to use these counters in real matchups
Apply healing reduction as your team commits damage. If he is also landing melee freely, add spacing and parries to the plan: anti-heal alone does not fix a losing close-range trade.
Kelvin sustains a fight inside his dome
Coordinate your anti-heal application and damage. Do not chase into a favorable dome fight just because you bought a healing counter; position and timing still determine who benefits.
Confusing a barrier or health swap with ordinary healing.
Applying anti-heal after the recovery window has passed.
Choosing a buildup item when you cannot keep landing shots.
What is the best anti-heal item in Deadlock?
There is no universal best option. Healbane fits reliable spirit application, Toxic Bullets fits repeated weapon hits, and Decay offers a targeted active. Choose the one your hero can deliver.
Does anti-heal counter every defensive ability?
No. Healing reduction does not automatically answer barriers, escapes, immunity or a health swap. Identify the specific reason a target survives.

role-frontline.title: How to Play Frontline in Deadlock | Deadlock Item Builder
role-frontline.meta: Learn how to frontline in Deadlock: create space, time engages, protect carries, manage cooldowns and choose durability for the damage you face.
blocks: How to Play Frontline in Deadlock
Give your team room to act. Good frontline play is about useful pressure, a survivable commitment, and knowing when to engage or turn back to protect an ally.
Give your team room to act.
Contest an approach your team needs

Your job is to make dangerous space usable. You might hold an entrance, threaten a charge, draw a defensive cooldown or interrupt someone diving your carry. The value is what your teammates can do because of that pressure.

Frontline is broader than “tank.” Durability helps you stay in the area, but enemies also need a reason to respect you: control, damage, displacement or a strong threat if they walk past. A durable hero far from the team can be ignored instead of creating useful space.
Heroes that can play this role
These are common playstyles, not exclusive classes. Your build and team needs decide which job to emphasise.
See how builds change these heroes’ jobs

Abrams[Frontline](/roles/frontline)Take space with close-range pressure and threaten a charge when teammates can follow.**Build emphasis:** Space and durability.[How to counter Abrams →](/counter/abrams)Baba[Spirit Carry](/roles/spirit-carry)[Frontline](/roles/frontline)Use spell pressure and transformation windows to contest space; empowered shooting changes the damage mix.**Build emphasis:** Ability damage or brawling.[How to counter Baba →](/counter/baba)Billy[Frontline](/roles/frontline)[Gun Carry (M1 Carry)](/roles/carry)Stay close enough to mix weapon pressure and melees while keeping a survivable route through the fight.**Build emphasis:** Close-range weapon pressure.[How to counter Billy →](/counter/billy)Infernus[Gun Carry (M1 Carry)](/roles/carry)[Frontline](/roles/frontline)Maintain hits to build damage over time; durability investment can support a closer brawling role.**Build emphasis:** Sustained damage and durability.[How to counter Infernus →](/counter/infernus)Kelvin[Support](/roles/support)[Frontline](/roles/frontline)Control an approach and protect teammates with healing, slows and a defensive fighting area.**Build emphasis:** Utility and space.[How to counter Kelvin →](/counter/kelvin)Lash[Spirit Carry](/roles/spirit-carry)[Frontline](/roles/frontline)Find an elevated approach and create an opening with a burst engage.**Build emphasis:** Ability damage and initiation.[How to counter Lash →](/counter/lash)Mo & Krill[Frontline](/roles/frontline)[Pick](/roles/pick)Approach dangerous space and lock down a priority target for teammates.**Build emphasis:** Durability and targeted control.[How to counter Mo & Krill →](/counter/mo-krill)Rat King[Frontline](/roles/frontline)[Support](/roles/support)Contest close space with rats and protection, using the banner to strengthen the area your team holds.**Build emphasis:** Durability and area utility.[How to counter Rat King →](/counter/rat-king)Shiv[Frontline](/roles/frontline)[Spirit Carry](/roles/spirit-carry)Apply pressure before committing into a close fight and threaten a finish on weakened enemies.**Build emphasis:** Brawling and ability pressure.[How to counter Shiv →](/counter/shiv)Silver[Frontline](/roles/frontline)[Gun Carry (M1 Carry)](/roles/carry)Build close-range pressure and commit when transformation gives a stronger chase and survival window.**Build emphasis:** Weapon damage and brawling.[How to counter Silver →](/counter/silver)Victor[Frontline](/roles/frontline)Occupy close space and turn a prolonged exchange into recovery and pressure.**Build emphasis:** Durability and recovery.[How to counter Victor →](/counter/victor)Viscous[Support](/roles/support)[Frontline](/roles/frontline)[Spirit Carry](/roles/spirit-carry)Save allies, disrupt an approach or invest in spell pressure; utility still matters in a damage build.**Build emphasis:** Saves, disruption or ability damage.[How to counter Viscous →](/counter/viscous)Warden[Gun Carry (M1 Carry)](/roles/carry)[Frontline](/roles/frontline)[Spirit Carry](/roles/spirit-carry)Combine weapon pressure and control, or commit around a stronger ability-based brawling window.**Build emphasis:** Weapon damage or sustained abilities.[How to counter Warden →](/counter/warden)Yamato[Spirit Carry](/roles/spirit-carry)[Frontline](/roles/frontline)Use lane pressure and a close-range spell sequence to threaten the backline during a strong survival window.**Build emphasis:** Ability damage and brawling.[How to counter Yamato →](/counter/yamato)

Use cover and pressure to help secure the wave. Threaten a close-range trade when the enemy has spent a key spell or stepped too far forward, but avoid losing half your health just to stand aggressively. Your partner must be close enough to benefit.

A missed engage often changes who controls the next few seconds. If your charge or other important approach fails, return to cover and resources instead of forcing another trade without the tool that made it favourable.
For the shared fundamentals, read the [Deadlock laning guide](/guides/laning-counterplay).

Move toward the space your team needs next: an objective entrance, a dangerous wave or an area your carry wants to farm. Check who is following before walking through the contested doorway. Being first only helps if the team can use the information and pressure.

Take accessible farm so you can survive your next job. Frontline does not mean permanently giving up souls, but it also does not justify consuming every safe resource while damage dealers are waiting for a spike. Prioritise the item that makes your next commitment workable.

Pressure can be enough without a full engage. Holding a threatening angle may keep enemies away from a wave or force them through another entrance. Stay ready to retreat if the teammates using your space have moved elsewhere.

Before engaging, check the distance to your follow-up and the enemy tools that punish you. A catch beside your team is often stronger than a deeper catch they cannot reach. Threaten the engage until you see a useful opening rather than spending it simply because it is available.

After committing, decide whether to keep pushing, hold the area or turn back. If an enemy bypasses you and reaches your carry, protecting that ally may matter more than chasing another target. You are still creating space when you use control defensively.

Use a route that lets you disengage or receive help. Drop behind cover when the enemy has spent pressure on you and your own survival tools are unavailable. Surviving the first commitment can let you return for the second opening.
How to choose items for your role

Buy for the damage and control you actually absorb. Healing reduction, sustained weapon pressure and spirit burst make different demands on your durability. Read the [shielding versus resistance guide](/guides/shielding-vs-resistance) before treating every defensive item as interchangeable.

A counter active can be useful when you can apply it while holding space. A personal control-prevention item needs to be used before the catch when its purpose is prevention; passive protection is more useful if you cannot reliably act in time. Compare [crowd-control answers](/guides/crowd-control) and keep enough threat that enemies must still respect your position.
Use the [Counter Item Helper](/counter-item-helper) to compare answers to the enemy heroes, then choose the purchase that fits your job.
Engaging beyond the reach of your team.
Taking damage in open ground without gaining space or forcing a useful response.
Chasing a backline target while your carry is being caught behind you.
Buying only health or damage without identifying why the last commitment failed.

On Abrams, holding a charge threat at an entrance can give your carry a safer firing angle. If the enemy walks past to dive that carry, turn the threat onto the diver rather than charging away from the fight your team needs to win.
[Back to the full hero roles chart →](/roles)
Is frontline the same as tank?
Not exactly. Durability is part of the job, but useful frontline pressure also needs a threat, control or displacement that lets teammates use the space you hold.
Should the frontline always start the fight?
No. Sometimes a pick teammate creates the opening, or you need to hold control for an enemy dive. Engage when the opening is useful and your team can follow.
Can a damage hero play frontline?
Some builds can, especially when close-range damage and survival tools let them contest space. Do not assume damage investment alone makes an unsupported dive safe.

item-maker.desc: Make a custom Deadlock item with editable stats and active or passive effects. Preview your item card and export a PNG to share your concept.

blocks: Make Your Own Custom Deadlock Items

The Deadlock Item Maker helps players create custom item ideas in a simple, structured format. Whether you want to experiment with new stats, invent unique abilities, or build item concepts for discussion, this tool makes it easy to turn your ideas into polished templates.

Instead of writing out item concepts in plain text, the Deadlock Item Maker gives you a cleaner way to organize your item name, stats, effects, and descriptions. This makes custom item ideas easier to edit, download, and share with other players.

Players can use the Deadlock Item Maker to brainstorm creative gameplay concepts, make theorycraft items, and explore how new custom items could fit into the game. It is a simple way to turn rough ideas into something more visual and shareable.
**Void Injector** – adds bonus spirit damage after dashing.
**Flux Engine** – increases mobility after using active abilities.
**Graviton Shell** – grants a temporary shield after taking burst damage.
**Pulse Anchor** – slows nearby enemies after activating an item effect.
Ready to make your own custom item? Use the Deadlock Item Builder to create a full item template and export it to share with the community.
faq: What is the Deadlock Item Maker?
The Deadlock Item Maker is a web-based tool that allows players to make custom Deadlock item ideas using an editable template.
Is the Deadlock Item Maker free to use?
Yes. The Deadlock Item Maker is completely free. You can make custom items, edit templates, and export your ideas without creating an account or paying any fees.
Can I download the items I make?
Yes. After making your custom item, you can export and download the finished template to share with friends, communities, or social posts.
Is this an official Deadlock or Valve tool?
No. This website and tool are fan-made projects created for the Deadlock community and are not affiliated with or endorsed by Valve Corporation.

What are the roles in Deadlock?

A role describes the job you are playing for your team: dealing sustained gun damage, creating spirit damage windows, taking space, catching targets, or supporting teammates. This guide groups those jobs into **gun carry, spirit carry, frontline, pick and support**.

These are practical playstyle categories. A hero can fill more than one role, and your build, available cooldowns and team composition can change which job matters most. Start with what your teammates need from you, then choose items that let you deliver it.
Find your hero to see common roles, your main responsibility and how your build changes the plan. Hero names open their counter matchup; role tags open the guide for playing that role.
Browse the heroes below. Some heroes fit more than one role.
